newsitem.title: USA: Fla. judge-electric chair not "cruel and unusual".
newsitem.headline: Fla. judge-electric chair not "cruel and unusual".

text.p: A Florida judge ruled Monday that the state's electric chair is not cruel and unusual punishment, clearing the way for resumed use of the device almost a month after flames shot from a convict's head during his execution.

Circuit Judge A.C. Soud rejected the claim of Leo Alexander Jones that use of the 74-year-old chair should be banned on constitutional grounds. Jones was sentenced to die for the 1981 sniper killing of Jacksonville police officer Thomas Safranski but Soud had stayed his execution last week to allow time for hearings on the electric chair.

The condition of Florida's electric chair became an issue on March 25 when a bolt of flame and smoke shot from the head of convicted killer Pedro Medina as he was put to death, the second time in 10 years flames erupted during an execution.
The incident prompted a debate over capital punishment and death penalty opponents expressed outrage over the chair, which prisoners carved from an oak tree in 1923.
"The Medina incident was the result of unintentional human error...," Soud said in a 15-page opinion. "But for the error, the execution would have been without incident."
Florida officials and doctors who examined Medina's body said a small sponge caused the fire after he was dead.

"Florida's electric chair in its present condition does not constitute cruel or unusual punishment," Soud wrote. He also dissolved a stay of Jones' execution, which has been tentatively rescheduled for 7:01 a.m. EDT on May 6, pending confirmation from the state attorney general.

But Jones will not be the next convict to test the chair. The Superintendent of Florida State Prison has scheduled the death of Gerald Eugene Stano for a murder in central Florida, for 7:01 a.m. EDT April 29. Stano has confessed to killing 41 women in Florida, New Jersey and Pennsylvania between 1969 and 1983.

"This ruling supports what our outside experts in electrical engineering had already found -- that the electric chair worked properly during the execution of Pedro Medina and that he died instantly," Florida Gov. Lawton Chiles said. He also noted the state had developed new procedures to avoid future problems with the chair.
